 9   Q.   What is the purpose of your testimony?

10   A.   I am testifying on behalf of CCAE to evaluate El Paso Electric Company’s

11        (“EPE” or the “Company”) proposals for serving large load customers, and

12        to recommend modifications that better protect existing New Mexico

13        ratepayers from cost shifts and stranded asset risks.

14               My testimony addresses five related areas. First, in Section II, I

15        provide background on the cost allocation challenges posed by large load

16        growth — including why traditional embedded cost approaches were not

17        designed to accommodate the scale and speed of data center load growth,

18        and what other jurisdictions have learned from their experience with large

19        load customers. Second, in Section III, I evaluate EPE’s proposed revisions

20        to its line extension policy, which addresses the incremental costs of

 5        I also recommend that the Commission direct EPE to file a proposal for

15        in Texas. Finally, also in Section V, I evaluate EPE’s proposed large load

16        tariffs — Original Rate Nos. 50 and 51 — including their exit fee, security

17        collateral, and minimum billing provisions. I recommend several

18        improvements to ensure that embedded cost recovery from large load

20   Q.   Can you summarize your key findings and recommendations?

 1   A.   Yes. My testimony addresses the cost allocation challenges posed by

 2        unprecedented large load growth in EPE’s service territory and

 3        recommends a series of modifications to EPE’s proposals that would better

 4        protect existing New Mexico ratepayers. My key findings and

 5        recommendations are as follows:

 6           •   Large load growth poses novel ratepayer risks that EPE’s
 7               current proposals do not adequately address. Data centers and
 8               other large load customers require infrastructure investments of
 9               unprecedented scale and speed. Traditional embedded cost
10               allocation approaches were not designed for this environment —
11               they can produce significant cost shifts from large load customers
12               to existing ratepayers in the near term and create stranded asset
13               risk if anticipated load fails to materialize. EPE’s proposals
14               represent a step in the right direction, but fall short of the
15               protections that this Commission should require.

16           •   EPE’s line extension policy does not adequately address shared
17               “but for” transmission costs. EPE’s proposed Infrastructure
18               Capacity Charge addresses only dedicated facilities — those built
19               solely to serve one large load customer. Shared transmission
20               facilities triggered by large load interconnection requests —
21               substations, transmission line extensions, and network upgrades
22               that would not have been built but for the large load — are
23               excluded and would instead flow into the rate base and be
24               socialized to all ratepayers. I recommend that the Commission
25               require EPE to implement CIAC with refund for all shared “but
26               for” transmission costs, identified through with/without load flow
27               modeling. I also recommend that EPE strengthen transparency and
28               oversight provisions for dedicated facility cost recovery, including
29               a defined methodology, repayment terms, and cost-recovery
30               guarantees for both the Infrastructure Capacity Charge and the
31               existing transmission voltage facilities charge.

32           •   EPE has not proposed a mechanism for allocating incremental
33               generation costs to large load customers. As large load

                                            6
                 DOCKET NO. 25-00082-UT
           DIRECT TESTIMONY OF RON NELSON

 1       customers require new generation to be procured — at marginal
 2       costs that may significantly exceed the system average — those
 3       incremental costs will be socialized to existing ratepayers through
 4       embedded rates. This is because ratepayers pay the average cost of
 5       the resources that serve them, and adding expensive new
 6       generation drives up the average cost through cost socialization, all
 7       things being equal. I recommend that the Commission direct EPE
 8       to file a proposal to directly allocate incremental generation costs
 9       to large load customers in its next general rate case.

10   •   Flexible service connections can reduce the costs and risks of
11       large load growth. If designed and implemented before large
12       loads connect to EPE’s system, flexible connections can defer or
13       avoid generation and transmission investments, reducing the costs
14       that large load customers impose on the system. I recommend that
15       the Commission direct EPE to immediately offer static flexible
16       connection options to large load customers and to develop a
17       dynamic flexible connection tariff within 6 months of this order.

18   •   EPE’s class cost of service study uses an outdated production
19       cost allocation method. EPE proposes to continue using a 4-
20       Coincident Peak — Average and Excess (“4CP-A&E”) method for
21       allocating non-peaking generation costs and the 4-Coincident Peak
22       (“4CP”) method for allocating peaking generation costs —
23       methods that over-weight coincident peak demand and fail to
24       reflect the time-varying nature of modern generation costs. I
25       recommend that the Commission require EPE to use the
26       Probability of Dispatch method, which would reduce the
27       Residential class cost of service by $8.3 million and better align
28       cost allocation with actual generation dispatch patterns, and direct
29       EPE to prepare new revenue apportionment and rate design
30       proposals based on the adjusted class cost-of-service results.

31   •   EPE’s jurisdictional cost allocation methodology does not
32       reflect the disproportionate concentration of large load growth
33       in Texas. EPE’s jurisdictional cost of service study uses backward-
34       looking test year demand allocators that do not reflect EPE’s
35       forecast that large load additions will be disproportionately located
36       in Texas. As Texas's large load demand materializes, New Mexico
37       customers will be allocated a share of infrastructure costs driven by

2                   to file a future rate case. I recommend that the Commission require
3                   EPE to file annual compliance reports that track actual large load

5               •   EPE’s proposed large load tariffs require strengthening. EPE’s
6                   proposed exit fees, security collateral, and minimum billing

24        II.   BACKGROUND: LARGE LOAD GROWTH AND COST
25                            ALLOCATION

26   Q.     What is the purpose of this section of your testimony?

27   A.     In this section, I provide background on the cost allocation challenges posed

28          by large load growth to help contextualize my evaluation of EPE’s specific

29          proposals. I begin by explaining the key cost allocation concepts relevant to

4    Q.   Can you provide any background on cost allocation that may be useful

5         as the Commission considers the Company’s proposals?

6    A.   Yes. Before I evaluate the Company’s specific proposals, I will first

7         comment on why historic approaches to cost allocation were not designed

8         to address the unique risks presented by large load growth. Considering the

9         Company's proposals within this larger context helps explain why EPE's

10        proposals, while well-intentioned, do not sufficiently protect existing

11        ratepayers from the cost shifts that unprecedented large load growth can

12        produce, and can illuminate lessons from other jurisdictions that this

13        Commission can draw from when evaluating the Company’s proposal.

14           b. Embedded, Incremental, And Hybrid Cost Approaches for
15              Large Loads

16   Q.   Are there any ratemaking concepts that are important to understand

17        data centers’ impacts on other customers’ rates?

18   A.   Yes. Average embedded cost of service, incremental cost allocation, or a

19        combination of both can be used to establish rates for new customers,

                                          11

                     DIRECT TESTIMONY OF RON NELSON

 1        including new data centers and other large load customers. Within the

 2        context of this proceeding, EPE’s line extension proposal is an example of

 3        incremental cost allocation, as it is intended to address the costs of

 4        incremental infrastructure constructed to serve a new customer; the

 5        Company’s large load tariffs are an example of embedded cost allocation,

 6        as they are intended to allocate historic (or estimated) infrastructure costs to

 7        large load customers. The cost allocation method a utility chooses will

 8        significantly impact the rates new and existing customers will pay, as well

 9        as the risks each customer type will bear. In particular, whether existing

10        customers are protected from short-term rate impacts and whether potential

11        benefits to other customers materialize over the long term are closely related

12        to how costs are allocated to new customers. This is particularly true for

13        new data centers or other large load customers that trigger extremely large

14        incremental costs to serve.

15   Q.   Can you explain how the average embedded cost of service method

16        works regarding large loads?

17   A.   At a high level, under an embedded cost of service approach, a utility

18        determines its total revenue requirement both for new investments required

19        to serve large loads as well as all of its historical investments in the electric

20        grid, functionalizes those costs into categories such as production,


                                             12
                             DOCKET NO. 25-00082-UT
                       DIRECT TESTIMONY OF RON NELSON

 1          transmission, and distribution costs, and allocates those costs to each

 2          customer class using allocation factors. 9 Allocation factors may be related

 3          to the number of customers, energy usage, maximum demand for each

 4          customer class, or other metrics. 10 The embedded cost approach treats new

 5          customers and existing customers the same, allocating costs to each in the

 6          same manner. 11

 7   Q.     Can you explain how incremental cost of service works?

 8   A.     Utilities can also allocate costs to new customers based on the incremental

 9          cost to serve those customers. Under this approach, the new load is directly

10          allocated the incremental cost to serve it in one or more functional

11          categories. While the customer will pay the incremental costs for new

12          resources, it may not be charged the costs of system expansion required to

13          serve subsequent new customers or the costs of the existing system.

14          Allocating the incremental cost to new customers can protect existing

15          customers from short-term rate increases and potentially insulate them from

16          the risks of stranded assets associated with large loads. However, existing

 3   Q.    Are there hybrid approaches that combine these two cost allocation

 4         approaches?

 5   A.    There are hybrid approaches to allocating costs, which draw on FERC cost

 6         allocation precedent for “but for” test for upgrades.

 7   Q.    What is the “but for” standard for identifying transmission upgrade

 8         costs that could be allocated to a specific customer?

 9   A.    The "but for" standard is the foundational principle of cost causation in

10         transmission interconnection at FERC. 12 Under this standard, a network

11         upgrade is deemed to be caused by a specific customer if that upgrade would

12         not have been constructed but for that customer's request for interconnection

13         or service. 13 Costs that meet the "but for" test are properly allocated entirely

14         to the cost-causing customer, regardless of whether other customers may

15         derive incidental benefit from the upgrade. 14

16   Q.    How does FERC allocate transmission costs that meet the “but for”

17         standard?

 1   A.   One method used by FERC is the "higher of" principle. This principle

 2        governs the rate a customer pays when it requests new capacity that

 3        necessitates incremental system expansion. 15 Under this principle, the

 4        customer seeking expanded capacity pays the higher of two amounts: the

 5        existing embedded system rate or the incremental cost of constructing the

 6        new facilities required to serve that customer's load. 16 The customer may

 7        not elect to pay only the existing system average rate when doing so would

 8        require other ratepayers to subsidize the incremental infrastructure costs

 9        triggered by the new customer's demand. 17

10   Q.   What is the policy rationale for the “higher of” principle?

11   A.   The rationale has two components. First, it enforces cost causation: a

12        customer who triggers new infrastructure construction should not be

13        subsidized by existing ratepayers simply because the incremental cost

14        exceeds the system average. Second, it prevents strategic behavior: without

15        the "higher of" floor, large customers could extract a subsidy by arguing

16        that they are entitled to pay only the embedded system average rate while

17        the incremental cost of serving them — which may far exceed that average

18        — is spread across all ratepayers.

16        For example, Contribution in Aid of Construction (“CIAC”) payments that

18        ensure that large loads bear all incremental costs as a floor while

19        maintaining the potential upside that can come from embedded rates over

20        the long term.

 1   Q.   Are there other hybrid pricing approaches for allocating transmission

 2        costs used by FERC?

 3   A.   While FERC policy prohibits “and pricing” where the same customer pays

 4        both an existing transmission rate and a separate new charge for the same

 5        transmission service or the same increment of capacity, there is no such

 6        prohibition from separating the cost of pre-existing shared infrastructure

 7        from the cost of new dedicated infrastructure triggered by a specific

 8        customer's interconnection request. 18 When the two components are

 9        properly disaggregated, there is no double-billing: one rate pays for pre-

10        existing network facilities that serve all customers, and the incremental

11        charge pays for new facilities that would not exist “but for” the specific

12        customer. Under “and pricing” the customer separately pays for its

13        incremental costs as well as embedded costs through separate rates. 19
